n: Let the KO clip play behind you. Straight to camera, calm. Let the number land.
p: That orange fighter is a neural network with about a hundred and sixty-nine thousand parameters.
It's beating the secret Hard final boss of a browser fighting game, and it's doing it with nothing but the keyboard.
In this video I'll walk through exactly how it works, step by step.

n: Set the constraints before the method. Count the three cards off.
p: First, the rules I gave myself. I wanted it to play like a person would.
It takes in 130 numbers: a summary of what's on screen.
It picks one of 17 moves, and that move becomes real key presses, fifteen times a second.
And it never writes to the game. No memory edits, no speed hacks. It reads the fight through the game's own read-only developer hook, which only exists on localhost, and it presses keys.

n: Point along the five boxes left to right. This is the map for the rest of the talk.
p: Here's the whole recipe in five steps.

A simulator built from the game's own code. A teacher: a search player that looks ahead. A student: a small net that copies the teacher. DAgger, where the teacher corrects the student's mistakes. And finally the keyboard, where the net plays the real game.
Let's go through them.

n: This is the trick most people find surprising. Slow down on 'the shipping fight logic itself'.
p: You can't train against a real browser tab at sixty frames a second. It's far too slow.

But I didn't write a simulator either. The game ships as a single JavaScript bundle, so I cut the bundle just before it starts touching the page, and exported the classes the fight runs on: Battle, Fighter, Bot, Match.
Then I faked just enough browser for it to load in Node, and swapped rendering, audio and models for a no-op proxy.
So the simulator is the shipping fight logic itself. There's no second physics model to drift out of sync.

Two changes make it usable for search. Gameplay randomness moves into a seeded generator, so the same seed and the same inputs give the same fight. And I can clone the whole fight state in about thirteen microseconds.
It runs at about forty thousand ticks a second, roughly six hundred and sixty times real time.

n: Quick slide. Gesture across the grid.
p: The net chooses between seventeen moves, all relative to the opponent, so 'forward' always means toward them.
Each decision covers four game ticks, which is fifteen decisions a second.
Directions are held for the whole window. Buttons are tapped only on the first tick, because the game reacts to the moment a key goes down.

n: Walk the four bullets, then point at the scoring formula. Emphasise the 1.25.
p: Before any neural network, I built a search player.
For every legal move, it clones the battle, reseeds the clone so the computer opponent reacts differently, plays the move, and simulates forty-eight ticks ahead with a simple scripted tail.
It scores what's left, and averages that over eight possible futures.
The scoring counts losing my own health one and a quarter times worse than dealing damage. Hold onto that; it matters later.
With eight samples and a forty-eight tick horizon, it beat the Hard boss four times out of five.
The problem: it's slow. Around eighty-one milliseconds per decision, and three and a half to eleven minutes of compute for one boss match.
At fifteen decisions a second you only get sixty-six milliseconds between decisions. The search alone needs eighty-one.
So the search player becomes a teacher. Every decision it makes gets logged: what it saw, the value of every move, and which move it picked. Then a small net learns to copy it.

n: Point at a few chips, don't read them all.
p: Here's what the net actually sees. A hundred and thirty numbers.
Distance, and for each fighter: position, velocity, health, meter, stun, what state they're in, which attack they're doing and how far through it they are.
Plus the round timer, rounds won, the arena pickups, hit-stop, and the previous action.
Everything is mirrored, so forward always points at the opponent. And the exact same file builds this in Node and in the browser, so training and live play see identical inputs.

n: For the ML people. Emphasise 'how much worse', not just 'which one'.
p: The student is a small MLP: a hundred and thirty inputs, three hidden layers of two fifty-six, seventeen outputs. About a hundred and sixty-nine thousand parameters.
The loss has two parts. A soft target, which is a softmax over the teacher's value for every legal move, so it learns how much worse each alternative is. And a hard target on the teacher's top pick.
It trains on a laptop GPU, exports to JSON, and runs in fifteen lines of plain JavaScript.
Two tenths of a millisecond per decision. About four hundred times cheaper than the search.

n: Pause after 'still lost'. This is the turn of the story.
p: And here's where it got interesting.
The student agreed with its teacher ninety-four percent of the time.
It still only beat the boss sixty-two times out of a hundred.
The reason: the teacher never wanders into the positions that the student's small mistakes lead to. So once the student ends up somewhere new, it has never seen a good move there. Errors compound.
The fix is a technique called DAgger.
Seven workers play matches where the moves are a fifty-fifty mix of the net and the search player.
Even when the net chose the move, the teacher labels every state it reached.
That gave seventeen thousand new labels, exactly in the states where the net used to fall apart. Then I retrained on all fifty-nine thousand.

n: Let the bars animate before speaking the numbers.
p: One round of DAgger.
Agreement with the teacher barely moved: ninety-four point three to ninety-four point nine.
Wins against the boss went from sixty-two to eighty-seven out of a hundred. Losses dropped from thirty-eight to thirteen.
And it still beats the other nine Hard opponents ninety-seven times in a hundred.
It didn't need to copy better. It needed to see more.

n: Have fun with this one. Smile on 'idle'.
p: Here's my favourite stat.
Ninety-three point six percent of its moves are idle.
About forty percent of those happen while it's locked into an animation anyway. But when it's truly free to act, it stands still ninety-five percent of the time.
It waits for the boss to commit, then punishes. It became a counter-puncher, and nobody programmed that. It inherited it from the teacher valuing its own health one and a quarter times more.

n: Combo clip plays on the right.
p: Then it plays the real game.

On every animation frame, an injected script reads the fight state, waits for the next four-tick slot on the game's own clock, builds the same hundred and thirty numbers, runs the net, masks moves that aren't legal yet, and holds or taps the keys.
For the recordings, Playwright drives Chrome, and I capture the game's own audio by tapping the Web Audio graph and lining it up with the video.
And it won.
Against the Hard final boss: two rounds to one, finishing the last round with ninety-eight HP left. Over eleven hundred decisions in under three minutes.
Against Hard Rahul: two rounds to nil.
Both fights are on the site, with sound.

n: Sincere, not apologetic. This builds trust.
p: To be honest about what this doesn't show yet.
Live, it has won two of four boss matches so far. That's well under the simulator's eighty-seven percent, mostly because browser timing isn't quite the same as the sim.
It has only faced the computer on Hard, never a human. Only one character was trained. And it reads state through the developer's localhost hook, though it still only ever sends keyboard input.

n: Back to camera. Point at the link. Hold two beats at the end.
p: So that's the recipe. The game's own code becomes a simulator, a search player becomes a teacher, a tiny net copies it, DAgger fixes its blind spots, and it plays with the keyboard.
The write-up, both fights with sound, and the code are at the link on screen.
Thanks for watching.
